failures.evidence: Every failure is `expected: <2026-09-09T20:31:06.968263928Z> but was: <...968264Z>` — the same field, nanosecond vs microsecond. The expected value comes from the POST /links response (`link.expiresAt()`), the actual from a later GET (`afterwards.expiresAt()`); the link was never modified (the patch was refused with 400/401/404). LinkService.java:82-95 builds the response from `Instant.now()`/`saveAndFlush(...)` without a DB re-read, while V1__initial_schema.sql:33 declares `expires_at TIMESTAMP(6) WITH TIME ZONE`, so the persisted value is rounded to microseconds and the create response is not. Two API reads of one immutable field disagree, which no reading of the contract permits; openapi.yaml:67 only says timestamps are ISO-8601 instants. Fix is implementation-side (truncate to the stored precision before responding).

Same defect as LinkExpiryTest: `assertEquals(created.createdAt(), performance.createdAt())` and the expiresAt equivalent (LinkPerformanceTest.java:48-49) fail with 534542534 vs 534543 — create response nanos vs GET micros. Contract behaviour B (AC7): 'The owner is shown the link's code, short URL, target, status, times and the exact number of clicks served.' The clickCount assertion passed; only the two timestamps differ.

'clicks counted before the outage must survive it: 3 became 0' (DegradedDependencyTest.java:174). The test used the contract's own outage mechanism, `TestInfrastructure.withCounterTierUnavailable` (harness item: 'pauses the Redis container through the Docker API and unpauses it in a finally block'), and asserted the contract behaviour verbatim: 'When the tier returns, clicks are counted again and everything counted before the outage is still in the total' (AC20, AC3). The loss is in implementation code either way: claim_click_deltas.lua removes deltas destructively while RedisClickCounter.claim (RedisClickCounter.java:84-90) swallows the timeout and returns Map.of(), so a command replayed after reconnect deletes deltas nobody writes down; and pendingDelta (RedisClickCounter.java:69-76) silently returns 0 on an unreachable tier, which makes the reported total go backwards. Medium rather than high because the read is taken immediately on unpause, so a reconnect race is a defensible alternative explanation.

Every failure is `{"error":"rate_limited"} ==> expected: <202> but was: <429>` on Bob's first report. Surefire runs classes alphabetically: AbuseReportRateLimitTest (properties ABUSE_REPORT_LIMIT_KEY=3, 8+6 reports as Bob) immediately precedes AbuseReportTest and leaves Bob's bucket at zero tokens. The contract anticipates exactly this — harness item: 'One Redis is shared by every context in the JVM, so buckets outlive a context: resetSharedTierState() flushes it, and each rate-limit class calls it in @BeforeEach' — but the reset is only in the drainer's @BeforeEach, so the drained state escapes to the next class. AbuseReportTest never establishes a bucket state and never resets. The implementation is behaving correctly: with the documented 60/min default (openapi.yaml:83) the bucket refills one token per second, and exactly one AbuseReportTest method (aReportAgainstAnotherCustomersLinkTakesItDown) got its 202 — a blanket implementation defect would have failed that one too. Repairable in author-tests (reset in @BeforeEach here, or in @AfterEach of the rate-limit classes); the contract only forbids resetSharedTierState in counting tests, and any reset here precedes the clicks it counts.

`NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "s" is null` at ApiClient.encode(ApiClient.java:315) via getLink/click — the link code is null because sign-in returned 429, not a token: ApiClient.signInFor (ApiClient.java:134-136) parses any body into SignInResponse without checking the status, so accessToken is null and every later call is unauthenticated. Same root cause as AbuseReportTest: SignInRateLimitTest (SIGN_IN_LIMIT_KEY=3, ten deliberate guesses, keyed by client IP per openapi.yaml:84) runs immediately before it alphabetically and leaves the shared IP bucket empty; the whole class ran in 0.035s, i.e. with no time for the 60/min refill. TenantIsolationTest declares no @BeforeEach reset and asserts nothing about rate limiting.

`Connection to localhost:5432 refused` from Flyway at AbstractRestartIntegrationTest.start(AbstractRestartIntegrationTest.java:112). That harness boots the app with `new SpringApplicationBuilder(...).properties(TestInfrastructure.springProperties())`, and SpringApplicationBuilder.properties() populates Boot's *defaultProperties*, the lowest-precedence source — below application.yml, whose `spring.datasource.url: ${DB_URL:jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shortener}` therefore wins. That line is frozen design content: it is present verbatim in the design commit c557a64's application.yml and untouched by the implement diff (23f0d0d changes app.* only). The corroborating symptom is that `server.port=0` is overridden the same way by `server.port: ${SERVER_PORT:8080}`. The implementer cannot reach src/test/** to fix it; the harness must pass these as command-line args or system properties.

The test asserts `assertEquals(postOnALiveCode.body(), postOnAnUnissuedCode.body())` (RedirectTest.java:336,339); the actual bodies are Spring's default error JSON and differ in `path` (echoed from the request) and `timestamp` (milliseconds apart) — they would differ on two calls to the same path, so the assertion is unsatisfiable against a default-dispatcher 405, and neither differing field discloses whether a code exists. The contract says both things: openapi.yaml:47 'Every non-2xx response has the ApiError shape. The catalogue is closed' (which the test and the test-contract behaviour 'refused identically whether or not the code resolves' rely on), and openapi.yaml:123 note 2 'Every other method on /{code} answers 405 from Spring's own dispatcher. No operation is declared for them' (which the implementation followed). The closed catalogue contains no 405/method_not_allowed code, so the ApiError shape cannot be produced for this status without inventing one, and the contract never states what the 405 body is. Both readings are defensible; a human should decide whether the dispatcher 405 is exempted from the ApiError rule or must be normalised.

summary:
23 failing methods across 7 classes, three distinct root causes plus one contract contradiction — this cannot be sent to a single branch.

IMPLEMENTATION (8 methods): create/patch responses report timestamps at nanosecond precision while GET reads them back from Postgres TIMESTAMP(6) at microsecond precision, so two API reads of one unchanged field disagree (LinkExpiryTest x6, LinkPerformanceTest x1). Separately, DegradedDependencyTest sees a reported click count fall from 3 to 0 across a Redis pause, which AC3/AC20 forbid; the destructive claim script and the error-swallowing pendingDelta read are both implementation code.

TEST (14 methods): AbuseReportTest and TenantIsolationTest fail entirely on 429s, because Surefire runs classes alphabetically and each is preceded by a rate-limit class that drains a shared Redis bucket keyed by the same identity — state the victim classes never establish and never reset. DurabilityAcrossRestartTest errors before it runs at all: its harness passes container coordinates through SpringApplicationBuilder.properties(), which are defaultProperties and lose to the frozen application.yml, so the app boots against localhost:5432. None of these are reachable by the implementer.

CONTRACT (1 method): RedirectTest's 405 body-equality assertion is unsatisfiable against openapi note 2 ('405 from Spring's own dispatcher') yet is what openapi's 'every non-2xx has the ApiError shape' and the behaviour statement demand — and the closed catalogue has no 405 code. A human decides which sentence governs.

If I am wrong, the most likely place is DegradedDependencyTest: the count is read the instant the container unpauses, and a Lettuce reconnect race would make that a harness timing defect rather than lost data. I would look at the service log for 'Lost N click(s)' or 'Could not claim click deltas' to tell the two apart before spending the implement attempt on it.
